blocks.content: In 2011, engineers at Heroku wrote down something most experienced backend teams already felt in their bones but had never fully named: there is a specific, repeatable set of practices that makes a web service easy to deploy, easy to scale, and easy to hand off to someone else at three in the morning during an incident. They called it the twelve factor app, and more than a decade later, in a world that has moved from bare servers to containers to Kubernetes, almost every one of the twelve still holds.

None of the twelve factors are exotic. Individually, most of them sound like common sense. What makes the methodology valuable is that it names the common sense explicitly, so a team can check a service against it the way a pilot runs a checklist, rather than relying on every engineer independently rediscovering the same lessons the hard way.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384671-533163485.png
blocks.alt: An app moves through build, release, and run as three strictly separate stages

blocks.content: 1. Where This Came From and Why It Still Matters
blocks.text: 1. Where This Came From and Why It Still Matters

blocks.content: Heroku built the methodology out of running thousands of different applications, in dozens of languages, on the same shared infrastructure. Anything that made one app behave unpredictably, keeping state on local disk, hardcoding environment specific values, needing a special startup ritual, made it harder to operate at that scale. The twelve factors are essentially the constraints that let wildly different applications all be deployed, scaled, and restarted the exact same way.

That same pressure exists today inside a Kubernetes cluster, even if nobody calls it a twelve factor checklist anymore. A pod can be killed and rescheduled onto a different node at any moment. A container image is expected to start from nothing and be ready to serve traffic within seconds. None of your application code gets to assume it knows which machine it is running on. The methodology predates containers, but containers ended up being the environment that enforces its rules almost by default.

blocks.title: One line summary
blocks.content: Build a service so that it does not care which machine runs it, how many copies of it are running, or when any single copy might be killed and replaced.
2. Codebase: One Codebase, Many Deploys

A twelve factor app has exactly one codebase tracked in version control, with many deploys of that same codebase running in different environments: one in development, one in staging, one in production. What varies between them is never the code itself, only the configuration and the running instance count.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396386004-476468274.png
blocks.alt: The same repository is deployed unchanged to every environment

blocks.content: If two services share meaningfully different code, they are not deploys of one app, they are two separate apps, and each one earns its own codebase and its own twelve factor discipline. A common early mistake is letting one repository quietly fork into environment specific branches that never fully merge back, which defeats the entire point: the whole value of "one codebase" is that the exact thing tested in staging is the exact thing that reaches production.
3. Dependencies: Explicit and Isolated

Every library a twelve factor app needs is declared explicitly, in a manifest like package.json, pom.xml, or requirements.txt, and nothing is assumed to already exist on the host machine. No relying on a system wide package that happens to be installed, no assuming a particular version of a language runtime is already present.

["Declaration: every dependency and its exact version is written down in one manifest file.","Isolation: dependencies are installed into an isolated location for this app, not shared globally with every other app on the machine.","No implicit system tools: even something as small as a shell utility used by a build script should be declared, not assumed."]
items: Declaration: every dependency and its exact version is written down in one manifest file.
Isolation: dependencies are installed into an isolated location for this app, not shared globally with every other app on the machine.
No implicit system tools: even something as small as a shell utility used by a build script should be declared, not assumed.

blocks.content: The payoff shows up the first time a new engineer clones the repository on a fresh laptop. If the app depends on anything not captured in its manifest, it fails to run for them, and that failure is actually useful, because it surfaces the hidden dependency before it becomes a production incident on a freshly provisioned server that is missing the same untracked tool.
4. Config: Store Config in the Environment
blocks.text: 4. Config: Store Config in the Environment

blocks.content: Anything that varies between deploys, database credentials, API keys, hostnames, feature flags, is configuration, and it belongs in environment variables, never hardcoded into the source. This platform already has a full Configuration Management topic covering the mechanics of this in depth, environment variables versus config files, secrets handling, validation at startup, and it is worth reading alongside this factor rather than repeating in full here.

The test the original methodology proposes is a strict one: could you make this codebase open source, right now, without leaking a single credential? If a database password is sitting in a config file committed to the repository, the answer is no, and that value has not actually been separated from the code, no matter how it is organized on disk.

blocks.title: A quick gut check
blocks.text: If the exact same build artifact, unchanged, can be pointed at a different database just by changing environment variables, config is correctly separated from code. If it requires a rebuild, config has leaked into the codebase somewhere.

blocks.content: 5. Backing Services: Treat Them as Attached Resources
blocks.text: 5. Backing Services: Treat Them as Attached Resources

blocks.content: A backing service is anything the app talks to over the network to do its job: a database, a cache, a message queue, an email provider, a payment API. The twelve factor methodology asks for a specific discipline here, treat every backing service as an attached resource, reachable purely through a URL and credentials stored in config, with zero code level distinction between a service you run yourself and one a third party operates for you.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396386006-838092226.png
blocks.alt: The application reaches every backing service the same way, through config, with no special casing

blocks.content: Done properly, swapping your self hosted database for a managed one, or switching from one queue provider to another, is a configuration change and a deploy, not a code change. The application code that reads from the queue never needed to know whether that queue lived on a server your team managed or inside a vendor cloud account, it only ever knew a connection string.
6. Build, Release, Run: Strict Separation

The methodology splits turning code into a running process into three distinct stages that are never allowed to blur together. The build stage takes the codebase and its dependencies and produces an executable bundle. The release stage takes that build and combines it with the configuration for a specific environment, producing a release that is ready to run. The run stage actually launches the app's processes against that release.

{"headers":["Stage","Input","Output","Can happen at runtime?"],"rows":[["Build","Codebase + dependencies","An executable build","No"],["Release","Build + environment config","An immutable, versioned release","No"],["Run","A specific release","Running processes","Yes, this is the only stage that runs live"]]}

Every release should be uniquely identified and, ideally, reversible: if the newest release breaks production, rolling back means simply running the previous release again, not starting a fresh build under pressure while an incident is active. Code that mutates itself at runtime, or a run stage that is allowed to make changes a rollback would not undo, breaks this guarantee.
7. Processes: Stateless and Share Nothing

A twelve factor app executes as one or more stateless processes, with nothing important kept only in that process's memory or on its local disk between requests. Anything that needs to persist belongs in a backing service instead, a database for durable data, a cache like Redis for shared session state.

This platform's Stateful vs Stateless Architecture topic covers the broader tradeoffs of this design choice in more depth. What matters specifically for this factor is the operational consequence: a stateless process can be killed and replaced at any moment, and nothing is lost, because nothing important was ever stored only inside it in the first place.

blocks.title: A common violation
blocks.content: Storing an uploaded file on local disk and reading it back later on the same server works fine in development and quietly breaks the moment there are two instances of the app running, since the second instance never received that file.
8. Port Binding: Export Services via Port Binding
blocks.text: 8. Port Binding: Export Services via Port Binding

blocks.content: A twelve factor app is completely self contained. It does not depend on an external web server like Apache or IIS being installed and configured on the host to expose it to the network; the app itself binds directly to a port and serves HTTP on that port, using an embedded server library as part of its own dependencies.

This is exactly what makes a service portable across environments without any host specific setup. One app can become the backing service for another app simply by being reachable at a URL, and that URL is nothing more than a hostname and the port the app bound to itself.
9. Concurrency: Scale Out via the Process Model
blocks.text: 9. Concurrency: Scale Out via the Process Model

blocks.content: Rather than making a single process handle more and more load by adding threads inside it indefinitely, a twelve factor app scales by running more copies of the same stateless process, spread across more machines, with a load balancer in front distributing requests between them.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396386007-4891596.png
blocks.alt: Load spreads across many identical, stateless process copies rather than one large process

blocks.content: This only works because of the factors that came before it. Processes have to be stateless, since a request routed to any one of them must get an identical result to being routed to any other. Config has to live in the environment, since every copy needs the exact same settings without manual per instance tweaking. Concurrency is less a factor of its own and more the direct payoff of getting the earlier ones right.
10. Disposability: Fast Startup and Graceful Shutdown
blocks.text: 10. Disposability: Fast Startup and Graceful Shutdown

blocks.content: Processes should be disposable: able to start in a few seconds, not minutes, and able to stop cleanly when told to, without corrupting data or dropping work silently. This platform's Graceful Shutdown topic covers the stop side of this in detail, draining in flight requests, closing connections cleanly, respecting a shutdown timeout, and is worth reading directly alongside this factor.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396386008-499614436.png
blocks.alt: A disposable process starts fast and shuts down cleanly on request

blocks.content: Fast startup matters just as much as clean shutdown, and for a related reason: an orchestrator that needs to scale up quickly during a traffic spike, or replace a crashed instance, is only as responsive as the slowest step in bringing a new process online. A service that takes two minutes to become ready effectively cannot absorb a sudden spike, no matter how many extra instances the orchestrator is willing to start.
11. Dev/Prod Parity: Keep Environments as Similar as Possible
blocks.text: 11. Dev/Prod Parity: Keep Environments as Similar as Possible

blocks.content: The gap between what an engineer runs on their laptop and what actually runs in production is where an enormous number of "works on my machine" bugs are born. The methodology pushes for closing three specific gaps: the time gap between writing code and deploying it, the personnel gap between the people who write code and the people who deploy it, and the tools gap between what runs in development and what runs in production.

["Time gap: deploy frequently, sometimes many times a day, rather than batching months of change into one high risk release.","Personnel gap: the engineers who write the code are closely involved in deploying and operating it, not handing it to a separate team that only sees it after the fact.","Tools gap: use the same database engine, the same cache, the same message queue in development as in production, not a lightweight stand in that behaves differently under real load."]
items: Time gap: deploy frequently, sometimes many times a day, rather than batching months of change into one high risk release.
Personnel gap: the engineers who write the code are closely involved in deploying and operating it, not handing it to a separate team that only sees it after the fact.
Tools gap: use the same database engine, the same cache, the same message queue in development as in production, not a lightweight stand in that behaves differently under real load.

blocks.content: Container based local development exists largely to close that tools gap: running the same Postgres image, the same Redis image, locally as in production removes an entire category of bugs that only ever show up because development quietly used SQLite or an in-memory cache instead of the real thing.
12. Logs: Treat Logs as Event Streams
blocks.text: 12. Logs: Treat Logs as Event Streams

blocks.content: A twelve factor app never manages its own log files, rotating them, deciding where they are stored, deciding how long to keep them. It simply writes every log event, unbuffered, to stdout, and treats logging as someone else's problem entirely. The execution environment is responsible for capturing that stream and routing it wherever it needs to go: a file, a log aggregation service, a long term archive.

This platform's Observability section already covers logging best practices, log aggregation, and correlation IDs in depth, and this factor is really the foundational assumption underneath all of it: none of that tooling can capture your application's logs in the first place if the app insists on writing them to a local file only it knows about.
13. Admin Processes: Run Them as One Off Processes
blocks.text: 13. Admin Processes: Run Them as One Off Processes

blocks.content: Occasional administrative tasks, a database migration, a one time data backfill, a console for poking at production state, should run as one off processes against a release, using the exact same codebase, the exact same dependencies, and the exact same config as the regular application processes. They are not a separate, drifting script maintained off to the side.

The risk this factor guards against is subtle but real: an admin script that lives outside the normal deploy pipeline can quietly fall out of sync with the actual application code, a migration script referencing a table structure the app changed months ago, still being run against production by someone who did not realize it was stale.
14. The Twelve Factors at a Glance
blocks.text: 14. The Twelve Factors at a Glance

15. Still Relevant in a Kubernetes World
blocks.text: 15. Still Relevant in a Kubernetes World

blocks.content: Every one of these factors maps almost directly onto a Kubernetes concept. A pod expects a stateless, disposable process that starts fast and shuts down gracefully on SIGTERM. A ConfigMap and a Secret are literally config stored in the environment. Horizontal Pod Autoscaling is the concurrency factor automated. A sidecar log collector shipping stdout to a central store is the logs factor, unchanged since 2011.

Some practitioners now talk about a "fifteen factor" app, adding factors around API first design, telemetry, and authentication and authorization as first class concerns rather than afterthoughts. That extension says less about the original twelve being wrong and more about how much of modern infrastructure was built assuming they were already true.
16. Common Questions

Does a twelve factor app mean no state anywhere in the system? No. It means the application processes themselves are stateless. State absolutely still exists, it just lives in a backing service like a database, purpose built to hold it durably, instead of in the memory or local disk of a process that could be killed at any moment.

Is this methodology specific to Heroku or to any one cloud provider? No. Heroku wrote it down first because their platform made the cost of violating it painfully obvious, but the principles apply to any deployment target: bare servers, Kubernetes, another cloud provider entirely.

Does dev/prod parity mean development and production must be identical? Not literally identical in scale, a laptop is not a production cluster, but as close as practical in the tools and versions used, so behavior differences come from data and scale, not from running fundamentally different software.

Why treat logs as a stream instead of just writing to a file? Because deciding how logs are stored, rotated, and shipped is an operational concern that varies by environment, and hardcoding that decision into the application couples it to one specific deployment setup instead of letting the environment handle it.
17. Key Takeaways

["The twelve factor app is a set of practices for building backend services that deploy, scale, and recover predictably, regardless of where they run.","Strict separation of build, release, and run makes every release identifiable and every rollback simple.","Config lives in the environment; backing services are reached only through config, never hardcoded.","Stateless, disposable processes are what make horizontal scaling and fast recovery from failure possible at all.","Logs are emitted as a stream, not managed by the app, so the execution environment can route them anywhere.","Nearly every factor maps directly onto a core Kubernetes or cloud native concept, which is why the methodology still holds more than a decade later."]
items: The twelve factor app is a set of practices for building backend services that deploy, scale, and recover predictably, regardless of where they run.
Strict separation of build, release, and run makes every release identifiable and every rollback simple.
Config lives in the environment; backing services are reached only through config, never hardcoded.
Stateless, disposable processes are what make horizontal scaling and fast recovery from failure possible at all.
Logs are emitted as a stream, not managed by the app, so the execution environment can route them anywhere.
Nearly every factor maps directly onto a core Kubernetes or cloud native concept, which is why the methodology still holds more than a decade later.

blocks.content: None of these factors are difficult in isolation. What makes them powerful is following all twelve together, since violating even one, keeping a bit of state in memory, hardcoding one config value, tends to quietly undermine the guarantees the other eleven were providing.
